# Introduction

Loops (`for`, `while`) are not the only way to repeat an operation in R. The **apply functions** applies a function over the pieces of a data structure and collects the results. The code is shorter, usually clearer, and avoids common loop bugs (forgetting to pre-allocate, off-by-one indices, etc.).



# The datasets

We use two datasets that ship with R

* `mtcars` — 32 cars, 11 numeric variables (mpg, cyl, hp, wt, ...).
* `iris` — 150 flowers, 4 numeric measurements and a `Species` factor.

```{r data}
data(mtcars)
data(iris)

# Make a few categorical versions of mtcars variables with readable labels
cars <- mtcars
cars$cyl_f  <- factor(cars$cyl)
cars$am_f   <- factor(cars$am, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Automatic", "Manual"))
cars$gear_f <- factor(cars$gear)

str(cars)
head(cars)
```

```{r iris-look}
str(iris)
summary(iris)
```

# `apply()` — over the margins of a matrix




## Column and row summaries

```{r apply-basic}
num <- mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt", "disp")]

# Column means  (MARGIN = 2)
apply(num, 2, mean)

# Column standard deviations
apply(num, 2, sd)

# Row-wise maximum for the first 6 cars (MARGIN = 1)
head(apply(num, 1, max))
```

## Passing extra arguments

Anything after `FUN` is handed to `FUN`:

```{r apply-args}
# Pass probs = to quantile()
apply(num, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))

# Round the results using the round() digits argument via an anonymous function
apply(num, 2, function(x) round(mean(x), 2))
```

## Functions that return more than one value

When `FUN` returns a vector of length *k*, `apply()` returns a matrix with *k* rows (for `MARGIN = 2`):

```{r apply-matrix-return}
apply(num, 2, function(x) c(min = min(x), mean = mean(x), max = max(x)))
```

Note for `MARGIN = 1`, the result is **transposed** (each row's result becomes a *column*), which often surprises people:

```{r apply-transposed}
head(t(apply(num, 1, function(x) c(total = sum(x), avg = mean(x)))))
```

## Applying to every cell: `MARGIN = c(1, 2)`

```{r apply-cells}
# Standardise (z-score) each cell using column statistics requires care;
# here is the simpler cell-wise example: convert weight (1000 lbs) to kg
wt_kg <- apply(mtcars[, "wt", drop = FALSE], c(1, 2), function(x) x * 453.592)
head(wt_kg)
```

## A practical use: standardising each column

```{r apply-scale}
z <- apply(num, 2, function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x))
round(head(z), 3)

# Verify: means ~ 0, sd = 1
round(apply(z, 2, mean), 10)
apply(z, 2, sd)
```

## Dealing with `NA`s

```{r apply-na}
m <- as.matrix(num)
m[c(2, 5), "mpg"] <- NA
apply(m, 2, mean)                 # NA for mpg
apply(m, 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE)   # na.rm is passed through ...
```

> **When to use `apply()`:** matrices and arrays. For plain data-frame column summaries, `sapply()`/`vapply()` are usually better because they don't coerce the whole data frame to a matrix. For simple sums/means, `rowSums()`, `colMeans()` etc. are much faster.

# `lapply()` — "list apply"

## Syntax

```r
lapply(X, FUN, ...)
```

`lapply()` takes a vector, list or data frame and returns a **list of the same length**, one result per element. A data frame is a list of columns, so `lapply(df, f)` applies `f` to every column.

## On a data frame (columns)

```{r lapply-df}
# The class of each column
lapply(mtcars[, 1:4], class)

# Mean of each column — returned as a list
lapply(mtcars[, 1:4], mean)
```

## On a list of vectors

```{r lapply-list}
my_list <- list(a = 1:10, b = c(2.5, 3.1, 8.4), c = c(100, 200, 300, 400))

lapply(my_list, length)
lapply(my_list, summary)
```

## Extra arguments and anonymous functions

```{r lapply-args}
lapply(my_list, mean, trim = 0.1)

lapply(my_list, function(x) x[x > 2])   # keep elements greater than 2
```

## Using an index: `seq_along()` and `names()`

Sometimes you need the *name* or *position* of each element:

```{r lapply-index}
res <- lapply(seq_along(my_list), function(i) {
  paste0("Element '", names(my_list)[i], "' has ", length(my_list[[i]]), " values")
})
unlist(res)
```

## Mixed column types (iris)

```{r lapply-iris}
lapply(iris, function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) round(mean(x), 2) else levels(x)
})
```

## Combining list results back into a data frame

Lists are flexible but sometimes inconvenient. `do.call(rbind, ...)` stacks the pieces:

```{r lapply-rbind}
stats_list <- lapply(mtcars[, 1:4], function(x) {
  data.frame(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), min = min(x), max = max(x))
})
stats_df <- do.call(rbind, stats_list)
round(stats_df, 2)
```

# `sapply()` — "simplifying apply"

## Syntax

```r
sapply(X, FUN, ..., simplify = TRUE, USE.NAMES = TRUE)
```

`sapply()` is `lapply()` followed by an attempt to simplify the list:

* every result has length 1 → a **vector**
* every result has the same length *k* > 1 → a **matrix** with *k* rows
* otherwise → stays a **list**

```{r sapply-basic}
# Length-1 results -> named numeric vector
sapply(mtcars, mean)

# Length-1 logical results -> named logical vector
sapply(iris, is.numeric)
```

```{r sapply-matrix}
# Length-2 results -> a 2 x n matrix
sapply(mtcars[, 1:4], range)

# Naming the pieces gives helpful row names
sapply(mtcars[, 1:4], function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), n = length(x)))
```

```{r sapply-list}
# Results of different lengths cannot be simplified -> list
sapply(list(a = 1:3, b = 1:5), function(x) x[x %% 2 == 0])
```

## Over a plain vector

```{r sapply-vector}
sapply(1:5, function(i) i^2)

# USE.NAMES = TRUE labels the result when the input is a character vector
sapply(c("mpg", "hp", "wt"), function(v) mean(mtcars[[v]]))
```

## A caution: unpredictable return types

Because `sapply()` decides how to simplify at run time, its output type can change depending on the input. On empty input it returns an empty **list**, not an empty numeric vector, which can break downstream code:

```{r sapply-pitfall}
sapply(character(0), nchar)       # list()   <- not numeric(0)!
class(sapply(NULL, length))
```

This is exactly the problem `vapply()` solves.

# `vapply()` — "safe" `sapply()`

## Syntax

```r
vapply(X, FUN, FUN.VALUE, ..., USE.NAMES = TRUE)
```

`FUN.VALUE` is a **template** describing what each call to `FUN` must return (its type *and* length). If a result doesn't match, `vapply()` stops with an error — better than silently producing a wrong structure. It is also slightly faster than `sapply()`.

```{r vapply-basic}
# Each call must return ONE numeric value
vapply(mtcars, mean, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1))

# Each call must return ONE logical value
vapply(iris, is.numeric, FUN.VALUE = logical(1))
```

## Returning several values

```{r vapply-matrix}
# Each call returns a numeric vector of length 2 -> a 2 x ncol matrix
vapply(mtcars[, 1:4], range, FUN.VALUE = numeric(2))

# Name the template to name the rows of the result
vapply(mtcars[, 1:4],
       function(x) c(min = min(x), median = median(x), max = max(x)),
       FUN.VALUE = c(min = 0, median = 0, max = 0))
```

## Behaviour on empty input — predictable!

```{r vapply-empty}
vapply(character(0), nchar, FUN.VALUE = integer(1))   # integer(0), as expected
```

## It fails loudly when something is wrong

```{r vapply-error}
# mean() returns a double, but we promise a character -> error
res <- tryCatch(
  vapply(mtcars[, 1:3], mean, FUN.VALUE = character(1)),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
res

# Wrong length: range() returns 2 values but we promise 1
res2 <- tryCatch(
  vapply(mtcars[, 1:3], range, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1)),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
res2
```

> **Rule of thumb:** use `sapply()` interactively for quick exploration; use `vapply()` in scripts, packages and anything that must be reliable.

# `split()` — cut data into groups

## Syntax

```r
split(x, f, drop = FALSE, ...)
```

* `x` – a vector or data frame.
* `f` – a factor (or list of factors) defining the groups.
* Returns a **list**, one element per group. `split()` does not compute anything itself; it prepares the groups for `lapply()`/`sapply()`/`vapply()`.

## Splitting a vector

```{r split-vector}
mpg_by_cyl <- split(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f)
mpg_by_cyl
```

## Splitting a data frame

```{r split-df}
by_cyl <- split(cars, cars$cyl_f)

names(by_cyl)
sapply(by_cyl, nrow)       # number of cars per cylinder group
head(by_cyl[["4"]], 3)     # the 4-cylinder cars
```

## Split, then apply (the core pattern)

```{r split-apply}
# Mean mpg per cylinder group
sapply(split(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f), mean)

# Several statistics per group, safely
vapply(split(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f),
       function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)),
       FUN.VALUE = c(n = 0, mean = 0, sd = 0))
```

## Fit a model per group

```{r split-model}
models <- lapply(split(cars, cars$cyl_f), function(d) lm(mpg ~ wt, data = d))

# Extract slope and R-squared from each model
vapply(models, function(m) c(slope = coef(m)[["wt"]],
                             r2    = summary(m)$r.squared),
       FUN.VALUE = c(slope = 0, r2 = 0))
```

## Grouping by more than one factor

```{r split-two}
g <- split(cars$mpg, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f))
names(g)
sapply(g, length)    # note: some combinations have 0 or very few cars
```

```{r split-drop}
# drop = TRUE removes empty combinations
g2 <- split(cars$mpg, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f), drop = TRUE)
sapply(g2, mean)
```

## Recombining results: `do.call(rbind, ...)` and `unsplit()`

```{r split-recombine}
# Summary data frame per group
summ <- lapply(split(cars, cars$cyl_f), function(d) {
  data.frame(cyl = unique(d$cyl), n = nrow(d),
             mean_mpg = mean(d$mpg), mean_hp = mean(d$hp))
})
summary_df <- do.call(rbind, summ)
rownames(summary_df) <- NULL
summary_df
```

```{r unsplit}
# Group-wise standardisation: z-score of mpg *within* each cylinder group,
# then put the values back in the original row order with unsplit()
z_within <- lapply(split(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f), function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x))
cars$mpg_z_within_cyl <- unsplit(z_within, cars$cyl_f)

head(cars[, c("cyl", "mpg", "mpg_z_within_cyl")])
```

## Using `split()` on iris

```{r split-iris}
iris_split <- split(iris[, 1:4], iris$Species)
lapply(iris_split, colMeans)

# Tidy into a matrix: species in columns
sapply(iris_split, colMeans)
```

# `tapply()` — apply a function by group

## Syntax

```r
tapply(X, INDEX, FUN, ..., default = NA, simplify = TRUE)
```

* `X` – a **vector** (one variable).
* `INDEX` – a factor, or a **list of factors**, the same length as `X`.
* `FUN` – function applied to the values of `X` in each group.

`tapply(X, INDEX, FUN)` is essentially `sapply(split(X, INDEX), FUN)`, but it returns an array whose dimensions correspond to the factors.

## One grouping factor

```{r tapply-one}
tapply(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f, mean)
tapply(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f, sd)
tapply(cars$hp,  cars$am_f,  median)

# Same result as split + sapply
sapply(split(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f), mean)
```

## Two grouping factors → a two-way table

```{r tapply-two}
tapply(cars$mpg, list(Cylinders = cars$cyl_f, Transmission = cars$am_f), mean)
```

Notice any `NA` cells? These are combinations with **no observations**. Control the fill value with `default`:

```{r tapply-default}
tapply(cars$mpg, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f), mean, default = 0)

# Count the observations in each cell to see where the gaps are
tapply(cars$mpg, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f), length)
```

## Three factors → a three-dimensional array

```{r tapply-three}
tapply(cars$mpg, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f, cars$gear_f), mean)
```

## Extra arguments

```{r tapply-extra}
# na.rm is passed on to mean()
mpg_na <- cars$mpg
mpg_na[c(1, 7, 15)] <- NA

tapply(mpg_na, cars$cyl_f, mean)                # NAs propagate
tapply(mpg_na, cars$cyl_f, mean, na.rm = TRUE)  # handled
```

## Functions returning multiple values

When `FUN` returns a vector, `tapply()` returns a **list-array** (not a matrix). Convert it with `do.call(rbind, ...)`:

```{r tapply-multi}
res <- tapply(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f,
              function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), n = length(x)))
res                      # a 1-D list-array
do.call(rbind, res)      # a tidy matrix
```

## Plotting `tapply()` output

```{r tapply-plot}
avg <- tapply(cars$mpg, cars$cyl_f, mean)
barplot(avg, col = c("#4C78A8", "#F58518", "#54A24B"),
        xlab = "Number of cylinders", ylab = "Mean mpg",
        main = "Average fuel economy by cylinder count")
```

# Putting it together: a full workflow

**Question:** For each cylinder group and transmission type, what is the average mpg, which group is most fuel efficient, and how does each car compare with its own group's average?

```{r workflow}
# 1. tapply: quick two-way table of means
means_tbl <- tapply(cars$mpg, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f), mean)
round(means_tbl, 2)

# 2. split: one data frame per (cyl, transmission) combination that exists
groups <- split(cars, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f), drop = TRUE)

# 3. vapply: safe numeric summaries for each group
summary_mat <- vapply(groups, function(d) c(n = nrow(d),
                                            mean_mpg = mean(d$mpg),
                                            mean_hp  = mean(d$hp),
                                            mean_wt  = mean(d$wt)),
                      FUN.VALUE = numeric(4))
round(t(summary_mat), 2)

# 4. Best group
best <- names(which.max(summary_mat["mean_mpg", ]))
cat("Most fuel-efficient group (cyl.transmission):", best, "\n")

# 5. lapply + unsplit: each car's mpg relative to its group's mean
rel <- lapply(groups, function(d) d$mpg - mean(d$mpg))
cars$mpg_vs_group <- unsplit(rel, list(cars$cyl_f, cars$am_f), drop = TRUE)
head(cars[, c("cyl", "am_f", "mpg", "mpg_vs_group")])

# 6. apply: summarise the numeric columns row-wise (a per-car "performance index")
perf <- apply(scale(cars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")]), 1,
              function(r) r["mpg"] - r["wt"] + 0.5 * r["hp"])
head(round(perf, 2))
```

# Comparison and choosing the right function

```{r comparison}
# The same task (column means) with every relevant function
a <- apply(num, 2, mean)                       # matrix-oriented
l <- unlist(lapply(num, mean))                 # list, then flatten
s <- sapply(num, mean)                         # simplified
v <- vapply(num, mean, numeric(1))             # type-safe

all.equal(a, l); all.equal(a, s); all.equal(a, v)
```
